title: The Book of All Duties
subtitle: How a Yadava minister tried to bind a kingdom into a single book of duty
era: Yadava scholarship and administration, c. 1259-1274 CE
moral: A state also survives in the manuals it leaves behind.

sources.note: Primary dharmashastra encyclopedia and source for Yadava genealogy, panegyrical in parts.

sources.citation: Hemadri, Ayurveda Rasayan, commentary on Vagbhata's Ashtangahridayam
sources.note: Attested medical-scholarly work from the Yadava milieu.

sources.citation: P.V. Kane, History of Dharmashastra, 5 vols (1930-1962)
sources.note: Standard contextual source for Hemadri's scholarship and citations.

panels.shot: low-angle three-quarter view, wide interior of a lamplit manuscript hall

dialogue.text: In the Yadava age of Devagiri, Hemadri Pandit dared to gather vows, gifts, law, medicine and royal memory into one vast book of duty—and hoped a kingdom could live inside its leaves.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye view over the plateau fortress and city below

dialogue.text: Mid-13th century Deccan. The Yadava kings rule from Devagiri, a hill of stone above a plain of trade. Here, a minister named Hemadri Pandit studies not only people, but the rules that claim to bind them.

panels.shot: medium interior shot, candlelit study with scrolls and icons

dialogue.text: Hemadri is a pandit and a minister. His world is filled with old dharmashastra texts—Manu, Yajnavalkya, countless commentaries—each prescribing duties, vows, gifts, penances. But they lie scattered, hard to wield in daily rule.

panels.shot: close-up on Hemadri’s face lit by the lamp, eyes intent

dialogue.text: He sees the gap: kings, priests, donors, pilgrims all ask, what is the right act here and now? The answers are buried across ages. Hemadri decides to stitch them together—into one Chaturvarga Chintamani, a ‘jewel of the four aims of life’.

panels.shot: wide interior shot of a court hall with scribes at work

dialogue.speaker: hemadri_pandit
dialogue.text: We will gather vows, gifts and expiations, sire—so no man must grope in doubt.

panels.shot: medium shot of Hemadri dictating, scribes in foreground

dialogue.text: Hemadri arranges his Chaturvarga Chintamani into sections—on observances and vows, on gifts of land and wealth, on expiation, on liberation. He does not erase the older voices; he quotes them line by line, preserving their words.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of a manuscript leaf

dialogue.text: P.V. Kane, centuries later, will trace countless lost works through these quotations. A Yadava minister, seeking order for his king, unwittingly becomes the archivist of India’s older dharmashastra memory.

panels.shot: medium shot in a temple courtyard, donors and priests present

dialogue.text: Gifts to temples, lands for brahmanas, vows taken by traders and widows—all pass through the language of dharma. Hemadri’s manual offers forms, precedents, promises of merit. It is law, ritual and royal policy braided together.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle shot in the court, Hemadri reciting genealogy

dialogue.text: Within his dharma-book, Hemadri praises his patrons. He recounts Yadava genealogy, their victories, their gifts as if cast in legend. These passages are panegyrics, not neutral chronicle—a minister’s tribute woven into a manual of duty.

panels.shot: close-up of a courtier whispering to another, Hemadri in background

dialogue.text: Later readers will mine these laudatory lines for Yadava history, but the record is bent by praise. Hemadri’s book shows not merely what happened, but how a court wished to remember itself.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a quieter inner room, Hemadri with a physician

dialogue.text: Hemadri’s hunger for system does not end with ritual. He turns to medicine, composing his Ayurveda Rasayan, a commentary on Vagbhata’s Ashtangahridayam. Here too, he links older knowledge to his own day.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of a medical diagram or verse

dialogue.text: In the Rasayan, Hemadri extends the classical medical tradition, glossing ailments, therapies, and the physician’s conduct. Law, ritual and healing all pass under his pen, as if the same idea of order ran through body and kingdom.

panels.shot: medium interior shot, Hemadri with visiting scholars and students

dialogue.speaker: hemadri_pandit
dialogue.text: Do not trust memory alone. Place each vow, each gift, where it can be found.

panels.shot: wide night-time shot of Devagiri’s ramparts under stars

dialogue.text: He serves under Mahadeva and into the early reign of Ramachandra. Beyond the walls, rival powers move—the Kakatiyas, the Delhi sultans—but Hemadri’s battles are with confusion, contradiction, forgotten precedent.

panels.shot: medium shot of storytellers later, pointing to a script scroll

dialogue.text: Later tradition will credit Hemadri with creating or standardising the Modi script. It is a good story for a learned minister, but no firm 13th-century evidence supports it; the earliest dated Modi records belong to much later days.

panels.shot: close-up of a cracked but legible Chaturvarga Chintamani leaf centuries later

dialogue.text: What survives securely is his writing. P.V. Kane, in the twentieth century, will sit with such leaves, reconstructing dharmashastra history through Hemadri’s quotations and arrangements, hearing across time the mind of a Yadava minister at work.

panels.shot: final wide shot blending Hemadri at his desk with faint outlines of kings and commoners

dialogue.text: The Yadava kingdom falls, its walls broken and palaces emptied. Yet Hemadri’s Chaturvarga Chintamani and Ayurveda Rasayan endure, showing how one court imagined right action—reminding us that a state outlives itself in the manuals it leaves behind.
